physiology.cardiac-cycle: One heartbeat is a sequence of filling and ejection: diastole, when the ventricles relax and fill, and systole, when they contract and pump.
physiology.heart-rate: How often the heart beats, set by the sinoatrial node and adjusted second by second by the autonomic nervous system and hormones.
physiology.blood-pressure: The pressure blood exerts on artery walls: systolic at the peak of ejection, diastolic between beats.
physiology.cardiac-output: The volume of blood the heart pumps per minute: heart rate multiplied by stroke volume, about five litres at rest.
physiology.cardiac-conduction: A wiring system of specialised muscle cells spreads each heartbeat from the sinoatrial node through the atria.
physiology.circulation: Two circuits in series: the pulmonary circulation loads blood with oxygen in the lungs, the systemic circulation delivers it to every organ.
physiology.breathing: Air moves in and out because muscles change the volume of the chest: the diaphragm and external intercostals enlarge it for inspiration.
physiology.gas-exchange: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the thin wall between alveoli and capillaries by diffusion, driven by differences in partial pressure.
physiology.oxygen-transport: Almost all oxygen travels bound to haemoglobin in red cells; how tightly it binds changes with the tissue's needs.
physiology.co2-removal: Carbon dioxide, the waste of metabolism, is carried mostly as bicarbonate and breathed out; the balance between the two sets blood acidity.
physiology.lung-volumes: The amounts of air the lungs move and hold, measured by spirometry and used to separate obstructive from restrictive disease.
physiology.neurons: The nerve cell: a body with branching dendrites that receive signals and a single axon that carries them onward, sometimes for a metre.
physiology.nerve-signals: Information travels as brief electrical pulses, action potentials, whose rate carries the message; at synapses it becomes chemical.
physiology.reflexes: Fast, automatic responses wired through the spinal cord or brainstem that protect the body before the brain has time to decide.
physiology.brain-functions: Different regions specialise: the cortex for perception, movement, language and thought; deep nuclei for movement and emotion.
physiology.sensory-systems: Receptors convert light, sound, chemicals, pressure and temperature into nerve signals that the thalamus and cortex turn into perception.
physiology.digestion: Food is broken down mechanically by chewing and churning and chemically by enzymes.
physiology.absorption: Nutrients cross the lining of the small intestine into blood and lymph; the colon reclaims water and salts.
physiology.gut-motility: Coordinated waves of smooth muscle contraction (peristalsis) move contents along the tract.
physiology.liver-functions: The liver processes everything absorbed from the gut, stores and releases fuel, makes most blood proteins, detoxifies drugs and produces bile.
physiology.pancreatic-functions: One organ, two jobs: exocrine cells pour digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the duodenum.
physiology.filtration: Blood pressure forces water and small solutes out of the glomerular capillaries into the nephron, about 180 litres a day.
physiology.reabsorption: The tubules reclaim over 99% of the filtered water and salt and all the glucose, and add wastes and excess ions to what remains.
physiology.urine-formation: Filtration, reabsorption and secretion leave one to two litres of urine a day.
physiology.fluid-balance: Water in equals water out: thirst, antidiuretic hormone and the kidneys keep the body's 40 litres of fluid within a litre of its set point.
physiology.electrolytes: Sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, chloride and bicarbonate carry charge.
physiology.hormones: Chemical messengers released into the blood that act on distant cells carrying the right receptor, coordinating growth, metabolism.
physiology.hormone-regulation: The hypothalamus tells the pituitary, the pituitary tells the glands.
physiology.feedback-mechanisms: Negative feedback, where a rise in the output switches off its own production, holds temperature, glucose.
physiology.endocrine-glands: Pituitary, thyroid, parathyroids, adrenals, pancreatic islets, gonads and pineal each make a signature set of hormones; several other organs.
physiology.gender-affirming-hormones: Feminising therapy (oestradiol with testosterone suppression) and masculinising therapy (testosterone) shift the body's sex-hormone environment…
physiology.menopause: The permanent end of periods when the ovaries run out of responsive follicles and stop making oestrogen.
physiology.menstrual-cycle: A roughly monthly cycle in which one ovary matures and releases an egg while the uterus builds a lining and then sheds it as a period if no…
physiology.pregnancy: From fertilisation in the fallopian tube to birth about 40 weeks later, pregnancy remodels almost every maternal system.
physiology.sex-hormones: Oestradiol, progesterone and testosterone are steroid hormones made mainly by the ovaries and testes under the control of the hypothalamus and…

symptoms.headache: Pain felt anywhere in the head.
symptoms.chest-pain: Pain or pressure anywhere between the neck and the upper abdomen.
symptoms.abdominal-pain: Pain between the ribs and the pelvis.
symptoms.back-pain: Pain in the spine or the muscles beside it, most often the lower back.
symptoms.knee-pain: Pain in or around the knee, the body's largest joint, where the femur, tibia and patella meet.
symptoms.shortness-of-breath: The sensation of not getting enough air.
symptoms.dizziness: An umbrella word for several sensations: vertigo (the room spins, an inner-ear or brain problem), light-headedness (about to faint.
symptoms.fatigue: Persistent tiredness that rest does not fix.
symptoms.nausea: The unpleasant sensation of being about to vomit.
symptoms.vomiting: Forceful emptying of the stomach through the mouth, a protective reflex run by the brainstem that closes the airway.
symptoms.fever: A body temperature of 38 °C (100.4 °F) or more, produced when the hypothalamus raises its set point in response to inflammatory signals.
symptoms.cough: A reflex blast of air that clears the airways of mucus, irritants and foreign material.
symptoms.rash: Any change in the colour or texture of the skin.
symptoms.numbness: Reduced or absent feeling in part of the body.
symptoms.tingling: Prickling, buzzing or crawling sensations without an outside cause, produced when sensory nerves fire abnormally.
symptoms.weakness: Loss of muscle power, distinct from tiredness or heaviness.
symptoms.joint-pain: Pain in one or more joints.
symptoms.breast-lump: A new lump, or an area of thickening that feels different from the rest of the breast, anywhere in the breast tissue.
symptoms.heavy-periods: Menstrual bleeding that is heavier or lasts longer than usual and gets in the way of daily life.
symptoms.pelvic-pain: Pain felt low in the abdomen, below the navel and between the hip bones.
symptoms.vaginal-bleeding: Bleeding from the vagina at a time when a period is not due: between periods, after sex.

conditions.coronary-artery-disease: Narrowing of the coronary arteries by fatty plaque (atherosclerosis), limiting blood flow to the heart muscle.
conditions.myocardial-infarction: Death of heart muscle because a coronary artery is suddenly blocked, usually by a clot forming on a ruptured plaque.
conditions.heart-failure: A syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs, or can do so only at raised filling pressures.
conditions.atrial-fibrillation: A common heart rhythm disorder in which the atria quiver chaotically instead of contracting, producing an irregular and often fast pulse.
conditions.hypertension: Persistently raised arterial pressure, usually defined as 140/90 mmHg or more in the clinic (135/85 on home readings).
conditions.deep-vein-thrombosis: A blood clot in a deep vein, most often of the calf or thigh.
conditions.pulmonary-embolism: Blockage of a pulmonary artery by a clot that has travelled from a vein, usually in the leg or pelvis.
conditions.stroke: Sudden loss of brain function because blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted, by a blocked artery (ischaemic.
conditions.migraine: A recurrent headache disorder with attacks of moderate to severe throbbing pain, typically one-sided, lasting 4 to 72 hours.
conditions.epilepsy: A tendency to recurrent, unprovoked seizures: bursts of abnormal synchronised electrical activity in the brain.
conditions.parkinsons-disease: A progressive disorder in which dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra of the midbrain are lost, causing slowness, stiffness and tremor.
conditions.alzheimers-disease: The commonest cause of dementia: a progressive loss of memory and thinking ability caused by the build-up of amyloid plaques and tau tangles and the…
conditions.asthma: A chronic inflammatory disease of the airways causing reversible narrowing, with episodes of wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough.
conditions.copd: Progressive, largely irreversible airflow obstruction caused by damage to the airways (chronic bronchitis) and destruction of alveoli (emphysema).
conditions.pneumonia: Infection of the alveoli, which fill with fluid and inflammatory cells so that part of the lung cannot exchange gas.
conditions.lung-cancer: A malignant tumour arising from the lining of the airways or alveoli, divided into non-small-cell (about 85%) and small-cell types.
conditions.appendicitis: Acute inflammation of the appendix, usually because its opening into the caecum is blocked.
conditions.gerd: Reflux of stomach acid into the oesophagus often enough to cause symptoms or damage the lining.
conditions.peptic-ulcer: A break in the lining of the stomach or duodenum that extends through the mucosa, caused by acid acting on a weakened defence.
conditions.gallstones: Hard deposits, usually of cholesterol, that form in the gallbladder when bile becomes supersaturated.
conditions.inflammatory-bowel-disease: Chronic inflammation of the gut driven by an abnormal immune response: ulcerative colitis affects the colon's lining continuously from the rectum.
conditions.colorectal-cancer: A malignant tumour of the colon or rectum, almost always arising from a benign polyp (adenoma) over years.
conditions.cirrhosis: Scarring of the liver from long-term damage, in which nodules of regenerating cells are surrounded by fibrous bands that distort blood flow and…
conditions.pancreatitis: Inflammation of the pancreas, acute when its own enzymes are activated inside the gland.
conditions.osteoarthritis: The commonest joint disease: progressive loss of articular cartilage with changes in the underlying bone, causing pain and stiffness.
conditions.rheumatoid-arthritis: A chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the synovial lining of joints.
conditions.osteoporosis: Loss of bone mass and deterioration of bone architecture that makes bones fragile and prone to fracture after minimal trauma.
conditions.fracture: A break in the continuity of a bone, from a hairline crack to a shattered, displaced or open injury.
conditions.acl-injury: A sprain or tear of the anterior cruciate ligament, the band inside the knee that stops the tibia sliding forward on the femur and controls rotation.
conditions.disc-herniation: Protrusion of the soft nucleus of an intervertebral disc through its fibrous outer ring, most often at the lower lumbar levels.
conditions.gout: An inflammatory arthritis caused by deposition of uric acid crystals in joints, triggered when blood urate is persistently high.
conditions.type-1-diabetes: An autoimmune disease in which the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas are destroyed.
conditions.type-2-diabetes: A metabolic disease in which the body's cells respond poorly to insulin (insulin resistance) and the pancreas gradually fails to compensate.
conditions.hypothyroidism: Insufficient thyroid hormone, most often because the immune system destroys the thyroid gland, slowing the body's metabolism.
conditions.hyperthyroidism: Excess thyroid hormone, most often from Graves' disease, in which antibodies stimulate the thyroid to overproduce.
conditions.urinary-tract-infection: Bacterial infection of the bladder (cystitis) or, when it ascends, the kidney (pyelonephritis), usually by gut bacteria such as Escherichia coli.
conditions.kidney-stones: Hard crystals, most commonly calcium oxalate, that form in the kidney and can pass into and block the ureter.
conditions.chronic-kidney-disease: Persistent reduction in kidney function (a filtration rate below 60 ml/min) or evidence of kidney damage such as protein in the urine.
conditions.anaemia: A haemoglobin concentration below normal (roughly under 130 g/L in men and 120 g/L in women), reducing the blood's capacity to carry oxygen.
conditions.sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated body response to infection.
conditions.breast-cancer: A malignant tumour arising from the cells that line the ducts or lobules of the breast.
conditions.cervical-cancer: A malignant tumour of the cervix, the neck of the uterus, that develops almost always from persistent infection with high-risk types of human…
conditions.ectopic-pregnancy: A pregnancy in which the fertilised egg implants and begins to grow outside the cavity of the uterus, most often in a fallopian tube.
conditions.endometriosis: A chronic condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus (the endometrium) grows outside the uterus, most often on the ovaries.
conditions.fibroids: Benign (non-cancerous) growths of smooth muscle and fibrous tissue that develop in the muscular wall of the uterus.
conditions.gender-dysphoria: The distress that can arise when a person's gender identity differs from the sex they were assigned at birth.
conditions.ovarian-cancer: A malignant tumour of the ovary or, as is now recognised for many cases of the commonest type, of the adjacent fallopian tube.
conditions.pelvic-organ-prolapse: Descent of one or more of the pelvic organs (the bladder, uterus, rectum, small bowel or, after hysterectomy.
conditions.polycystic-ovary-syndrome: A common hormonal condition in which the ovaries make more androgens (hormones such as testosterone, which everyone makes.
conditions.urinary-incontinence: The involuntary leakage of urine, from an occasional dribble on coughing to a complete loss of bladder control.
conditions.angina: Angina is chest pain or discomfort that happens when the heart muscle does not get enough blood.
conditions.diverticulitis: Diverticular disease is a condition in which small pouches in the wall of the large intestine cause symptoms.
conditions.fatty-liver-disease: A common condition in which fat builds up in the liver, often linked to being overweight.
conditions.influenza: Flu is a respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses.
conditions.irritable-bowel-syndrome: A long-term digestive condition with repeated abdominal pain and changes in bowel habit, but no visible damage or disease in the digestive tract.
conditions.multiple-sclerosis: A lifelong condition in which the immune system mistakenly attacks nerves in the brain and spinal cord.
conditions.norovirus: A highly contagious viral infection of the gut that causes sudden vomiting and diarrhoea.
conditions.shingles: Shingles is a painful rash caused by the chickenpox virus becoming active again after lying dormant in the body.
conditions.lupus: A long-term autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks healthy tissue, most often causing joint aches, skin rashes and tiredness.
conditions.fibromyalgia: A long-term condition that causes pain all over the body.
conditions.vertigo: Vertigo is the feeling that you, or the world around you, is moving or spinning, and it is often caused by a problem in the inner ear.
conditions.lactose-intolerance: Digestive symptoms such as bloating, diarrhoea and gas that follow eating or drinking foods that contain lactose, the sugar in milk.
conditions.vitamin-d-deficiency: A shortage of vitamin D in the body, which can weaken bones and muscles over time.
conditions.vitamin-b12-deficiency: A lack of vitamin B12 or folate that affects the body's ability to make fully working red blood cells.
conditions.hernia: A hernia forms when muscle weakness lets tissue push through.
conditions.sciatica: Pain, and sometimes tingling, numbness or weakness, in one leg when the sciatic nerve is irritated or compressed.
conditions.high-cholesterol: High cholesterol, also called hypercholesterolaemia, means there is too much cholesterol in the blood.
conditions.coeliac-disease: Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system reacts to gluten and damages the lining of the small bowel.
conditions.hepatitis-c: Hepatitis C is an infection with a virus that causes inflammation of the liver, which can damage the liver over time.
conditions.sinusitis: Sinusitis is inflammation of the sinuses, usually caused by an infection.
conditions.bronchitis: Bronchitis is inflammation of the airways in the lungs, usually caused by an infection.
conditions.sleep-apnoea: Obstructive sleep apnoea is a condition in which the throat narrows or closes during sleep, so breathing stops and starts again.
conditions.aortic-aneurysm: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is a bulge in the aorta, the body's main blood vessel, where it runs through the tummy.
conditions.peripheral-arterial-disease: A long-term condition in which the arteries that supply blood to the legs become narrowed or blocked.
conditions.covid-19: COVID-19 is an illness caused by a virus called coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2), with symptoms that overlap with colds and flu.
conditions.chlamydia: A sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis.
conditions.kidney-infection: A kidney infection, also called pyelonephritis, is a urinary tract infection that affects one or both kidneys.
conditions.tonsillitis: An infection of the tonsils, most often caused by a virus and sometimes by bacteria, that brings a sore throat, painful swallowing and fever.
conditions.ear-infection: An ear infection is an infection, usually of the middle ear behind the eardrum, that is common in children and often settles without treatment.
conditions.thrush: A common yeast infection caused by Candida, a fungus that normally lives harmlessly on the body, which can affect the mouth.
conditions.meningitis: Meningitis is an infection of the protective membranes that surround the brain and spinal cord.
conditions.hiv: HIV is a virus that attacks the immune system and, with treatment, can be managed as a long-term condition.
conditions.anxiety-disorders: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is a long-term condition in which a person feels worried or anxious about many different things, much of the time.
conditions.depression: Depression is a low mood that lasts for weeks or months and affects daily life.
conditions.adhd: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects attention, activity levels and impulse control.
conditions.autism: A lifelong difference in how a person communicates, behaves and reacts compared with people who are not autistic.
conditions.ocd: Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) is a mental health condition in which a person has obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours.
conditions.ptsd: A mental health condition that can develop after very stressful, frightening or distressing events.
conditions.bipolar-disorder: Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition that causes extreme mood changes, with high moods (mania or hypomania) and low moods (depression).
conditions.insomnia: A sleep problem in which a person regularly has trouble sleeping, including finding it hard to get to sleep or waking often in the night.
conditions.menopause: Menopause is when periods stop altogether, and perimenopause is the stage before this when periods change and symptoms begin.
conditions.erectile-dysfunction: Erectile dysfunction, also called impotence, is being unable to get or keep an erection.
conditions.enlarged-prostate: An enlarged prostate is a common condition in which the prostate gland grows larger and can squeeze the urethra, the outlet tube for urine.
conditions.gonorrhoea: A bacterial sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae that can affect the genitals, rectum, throat and eyes.
conditions.genital-herpes: Genital herpes is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the herpes simplex virus.
conditions.pre-eclampsia: Pre-eclampsia is a condition that can develop in pregnancy, with high blood pressure and protein in the urine as its early signs.
conditions.gestational-diabetes: Gestational diabetes is a form of diabetes that starts during pregnancy and typically clears up after the baby is born.
conditions.pancreatic-cancer: Pancreatic cancer is a cancer that starts in the pancreas, an organ that helps with digestion.
conditions.prostate-cancer: Prostate cancer is a cancer that starts in the prostate, a small gland in the male reproductive system that sits just below the bladder.
conditions.lymphoma: Lymphoma is a cancer of the lymphatic system, and doctors group it into Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
conditions.skin-cancer: Skin cancer is a group of cancers that start in the skin, divided into melanoma and non-melanoma types.
conditions.thyroid-cancer: Thyroid cancer is a cancer that starts in the thyroid gland, a gland in the neck that makes hormones.
conditions.bladder-cancer: Bladder cancer is cancer that forms in the tissues of the bladder, the organ that stores urine.
conditions.testicular-cancer: Testicular cancer is a cancer that starts in a testicle, one of the two glands in the scrotum.
conditions.brain-tumour: A brain tumour is a growth of abnormal cells in or around the brain, and it may be non-cancerous or cancerous.
conditions.eczema: A skin condition that causes dry, itchy skin and comes and goes in flare-ups.
conditions.psoriasis: A long-term inflammatory skin condition in which the immune system is involved, usually showing as raised red patches covered with silvery scales.
conditions.acne: Acne is a common skin condition in which spots, from a few small ones to deep painful lumps, appear mostly on the face, chest and back.
conditions.hives: Hives, also called urticaria or nettle rash, is an itchy, raised rash that can appear anywhere on the body.
conditions.hay-fever: Hay fever is an allergic reaction to pollen, also called seasonal allergic rhinitis.
conditions.food-allergy: A food allergy is when the immune system overreacts to certain foods, with reactions that range from mild to life-threatening anaphylaxis.
conditions.cellulitis: Cellulitis is an infection of the deeper layers of the skin caused by bacteria.
conditions.conjunctivitis: Inflammation of the conjunctiva, the clear tissue that covers the white of the eye and lines the inside of the eyelids.

tests.complete-blood-count: The most commonly ordered blood test: an automated count of the red cells, white cells and platelets in a small sample.
tests.blood-glucose: The concentration of glucose in blood, measured from a vein or a fingerprick.
tests.hba1c: The fraction of haemoglobin that has glucose stuck to it.
tests.liver-function-tests: A panel of enzymes and proteins that together show whether liver cells are injured, whether bile is flowing.
tests.kidney-function-tests: Creatinine and urea are waste products the kidneys should clear; how much builds up in blood shows how well they are filtering.
tests.lipid-profile: Measures the fats carried in blood: total cholesterol, LDL ('bad', deposited in artery walls), HDL ('good'.
tests.electrolytes: The dissolved salts that set the water content of the body and the electrical behaviour of nerves, muscle and the heart: sodium, potassium, chloride.
tests.thyroid-function-tests: TSH from the pituitary and the thyroid hormones T4 and T3 measured together.
tests.hormone-tests: Blood levels of hormones and related chemicals, interpreted against the time of day.
tests.urinalysis: A plastic strip with chemical pads dipped into a fresh urine sample.
tests.urine-culture: A urine sample is spread on culture plates and incubated for 24-48 hours to grow any bacteria, identify them and test which antibiotics kill them.
tests.urine-protein: Healthy kidney filters hold back almost all protein.
tests.pregnancy-test: Detects human chorionic gonadotropin, a hormone that begins to be made in the days after fertilisation, as the embryo implants in the womb.
tests.ecg: Ten sticky electrodes on the chest and limbs record the heart's electrical activity from twelve angles over ten seconds.
tests.echocardiogram: An ultrasound of the beating heart.
tests.stress-test: The heart is made to work hard, by treadmill or bicycle exercise or by a drug that mimics exercise, while its electrical activity.
tests.holter-monitor: A portable recorder worn for 24 hours to two weeks (or an implanted loop recorder for up to three years) that captures the heart's rhythm during…
tests.spirometry: A forced breath out into a tube measures how much air the lungs can move and how fast.
tests.pulmonary-function-tests: Spirometry plus measurements it cannot make: the total volume of the lungs including the air that cannot be blown out.
tests.pulse-oximetry: A clip on the fingertip shines red and infrared light through the tissue and reads the colour of pulsing blood to estimate how saturated haemoglobin…
tests.endoscopy: A flexible or rigid tube with a light and camera passed into a body cavity through a natural opening or a small cut.
tests.biopsy: Removal of a small piece of tissue or a few cells so a pathologist can examine them under the microscope.
tests.genetic-testing: Reading part or all of a person's DNA (from blood or saliva) or a tumour's DNA (from a biopsy) to find variants that cause disease, raise risk.
tests.microbiology-tests: Tests that find the organism causing an infection: growing it on culture, detecting its genes by PCR, its proteins by antigen tests.
tests.troponin: A blood test for cardiac troponin, a protein released when heart muscle cells are injured.
tests.bnp: A blood test for the natriuretic peptides the heart's ventricles release when they are stretched by high pressure or extra volume.
tests.crp: A blood test for C-reactive protein, a protein the liver releases within hours of significant inflammation, infection or tissue injury.
tests.esr: An old but still useful test that measures how far red blood cells settle in a narrow tube in one hour.
tests.tsh: The single most sensitive blood test of thyroid function: TSH from the pituitary rises when the thyroid is underactive and falls when it is…
tests.ferritin: A blood test that estimates the body's iron stores by measuring ferritin, the protein that holds iron inside cells.
tests.creatinine-egfr: The everyday measure of how well the kidneys filter.
tests.prothrombin-time-inr: The prothrombin time measures how many seconds plasma takes to clot once the tissue-factor pathway is triggered.
tests.iron-studies: A group of blood tests that together describe how much iron the body has stored.
tests.vitamin-b12-folate: Two blood tests, usually ordered together, for the vitamins the bone marrow needs to make normal red cells and the nervous system needs to keep…
tests.vitamin-d: Measures 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the storage form the liver makes from vitamin D obtained from sunlight on skin and from food or supplements.
tests.hepatitis-b-serology: A set of blood tests that shows whether someone has hepatitis B now, had it in the past, is immune from vaccination, or carries the virus long term.
tests.hiv-test: A blood test that looks for the human immunodeficiency virus.
tests.blood-pressure-measurement: The pressure of blood against the artery walls, recorded as two numbers: the systolic pressure when the heart contracts and the diastolic pressure…
tests.cervical-screening: A sample of cells brushed from the transformation zone of the cervix.

imaging.x-ray: The oldest and most widely available imaging test: a brief beam of X-rays casts a shadow picture of bone, air and soft tissue, ideal for fractures.
imaging.ct-scan: A rotating X-ray tube and computer build cross-sectional slices of the body in seconds, showing bone, organs.
imaging.mri: Magnetic resonance imaging uses a strong magnet and radio waves, not radiation, to produce detailed pictures of soft tissue: the brain, spinal cord.
imaging.ultrasound: High-frequency sound waves bounced off tissue give real-time, radiation-free images, used for pregnancy, the abdomen, the heart (echocardiography).
imaging.pet-scan: Positron emission tomography tracks a mildly radioactive sugar or tracer to show where cells are most active.
imaging.mammography: A low-dose X-ray of the compressed breast that can detect cancers years before they can be felt.
imaging.fluoroscopy: Continuous X-ray imaging shown as a live moving picture, used to watch swallowing.
imaging.dxa-scan: A quick, very low-dose X-ray measurement of bone mineral density at the hip and spine, reported as a T-score.

procedures.appendectomy: Surgical removal of the inflamed appendix, usually by keyhole surgery, is the standard treatment for acute appendicitis.
procedures.cholecystectomy: Keyhole removal of the gallbladder is the usual treatment for gallstones that cause pain or complications; the liver keeps making bile.
procedures.knee-replacement: The worn joint surfaces of the knee are replaced with metal components and a polyethylene insert to relieve the pain of severe arthritis when…
procedures.cataract-surgery: The eye's clouded natural lens is broken up with ultrasound through a tiny corneal incision and replaced with a folded artificial lens.
procedures.angioplasty: A balloon and stent passed through a catheter from the wrist or groin reopen a narrowed or blocked coronary artery.
procedures.coronary-bypass: Open-heart surgery that bypasses blocked coronary arteries with the patient's own chest-wall artery and leg vein or arm artery.
procedures.cardiac-catheterization: Thin catheters passed from the wrist or groin to the heart measure chamber pressures, film the coronary arteries with contrast dye and.
procedures.upper-endoscopy: A flexible camera passed through the mouth examines the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum, allowing biopsies and treatment.
procedures.colonoscopy: A flexible camera is passed around the whole large intestine after laxative bowel preparation to find and remove polyps.
procedures.bronchoscopy: A thin flexible scope is passed through the nose or mouth, between the vocal cords and down the trachea into the bronchi of each lung.
procedures.dialysis: Dialysis takes over the kidneys' filtering work when they have failed.
procedures.blood-transfusion: Donated red cells, platelets or plasma are given into a vein, matched to the recipient's blood group and checked at every step, to treat anaemia.
procedures.urinary-catheterization: A soft tube passed along the urethra (or through the lower abdomen) into the bladder drains urine when the bladder cannot empty or output must be…
procedures.joint-aspiration: A needle drawn into a swollen joint removes fluid for analysis and relief of pressure, and may be followed by a corticosteroid injection.
procedures.caesarean-section: Birth of a baby through a cut in the lower abdomen and in the lower segment of the uterus.
procedures.chest-masculinisation: Removal of most of the breast tissue and excess skin, with resizing and repositioning of the nipples, to give a flat chest with a male contour.
procedures.phalloplasty: Construction of a penis, most often as gender-affirming surgery for trans men and some non-binary people assigned female at birth.
procedures.vaginoplasty: Construction of a vagina and vulva, most often as gender-affirming surgery for trans women and some non-binary people.

medications.aspirin: A low-dose antiplatelet that stops platelets clumping into clots, used long term after heart attacks and strokes.
medications.ibuprofen: A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAID) that eases pain, inflammation and fever by blocking prostaglandin production.
medications.paracetamol: The first-line painkiller and fever reducer for most people (acetaminophen in North America).
medications.morphine: The reference strong opioid for severe pain, such as after major surgery, injury or in advanced cancer; highly effective but sedating.
medications.atorvastatin: A high-intensity statin that lowers LDL cholesterol by blocking its production in the liver.
medications.ramipril: An ACE inhibitor that relaxes blood vessels and eases the heart's workload, used for high blood pressure, heart failure.
medications.metoprolol: A beta blocker that slows the heart and reduces its oxygen demand, used for angina, after heart attacks.
medications.amlodipine: A long-acting calcium channel blocker that relaxes artery walls to lower blood pressure and prevent angina.
medications.furosemide: A powerful loop diuretic that makes the kidneys excrete salt and water within an hour, used to clear fluid overload in heart failure.
medications.glyceryl-trinitrate: A fast-acting nitrate spray or tablet under the tongue that widens veins and coronary arteries to relieve an angina attack within minutes.
medications.apixaban: A direct oral anticoagulant that blocks clotting factor Xa, preventing strokes in atrial fibrillation and treating deep vein thrombosis and…
medications.warfarin: The long-established oral anticoagulant that blocks vitamin K-dependent clotting factors.
medications.metformin: The first-line tablet for type 2 diabetes: it reduces the glucose the liver releases and improves the body's response to insulin.
medications.insulin: The hormone that moves glucose from the blood into cells, given by injection or pump to everyone with type 1 diabetes and to many with type 2 when…
medications.levothyroxine: Synthetic thyroid hormone (T4) that replaces what an underactive thyroid cannot make, restoring energy, weight and metabolism.
medications.salbutamol: The blue reliever inhaler: a short-acting beta-2 agonist that opens the airways within minutes to relieve asthma and COPD symptoms during an attack…
medications.inhaled-corticosteroids: The preventer inhalers of asthma: low doses of steroid delivered straight into the airways damp down inflammation so attacks become rarer and milder.
medications.omeprazole: A proton pump inhibitor that switches off acid production in the stomach.
medications.amoxicillin: A widely used penicillin antibiotic that kills bacteria by breaking their cell walls, prescribed for chest, ear, sinus.
medications.cetirizine: A second-generation (less sedating) antihistamine that blocks histamine H1 receptors to relieve hay fever, hives and other allergic symptoms.
medications.sertraline: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) antidepressant used for depression, anxiety disorders, panic and obsessive-compulsive disorder.
medications.prednisolone: A corticosteroid tablet that suppresses inflammation and the immune system, used in asthma flare-ups, arthritis.
medications.allopurinol: A xanthine oxidase inhibitor that lowers uric acid in the blood.
medications.alendronate: A weekly bisphosphonate that slows bone breakdown, strengthening bone in osteoporosis and cutting the risk of hip and spine fractures.
medications.losartan: An angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) that relaxes blood vessels to lower blood pressure and protect the kidneys in diabetes.
medications.lisinopril: An ACE inhibitor that lowers blood pressure, protects the heart after a heart attack and in heart failure.
medications.rosuvastatin: A high-intensity statin that lowers LDL cholesterol by more, milligram for milligram, than any other statin.
medications.azithromycin: A macrolide antibiotic that stops bacteria making proteins, given as a short course (often three days) for chest, ear, sinus.
medications.clopidogrel: An antiplatelet medicine that stops platelets clumping by blocking their P2Y12 receptor, taken to prevent clots after a heart attack, stent.
medications.bisoprolol: A once-daily beta blocker that selectively slows the heart and lowers its workload, used for heart failure, angina.
medications.citalopram: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor antidepressant used for depression and panic disorder, taken once daily.
medications.clarithromycin: A macrolide antibiotic for chest, skin, ear and throat infections and part of the combination that eradicates Helicobacter pylori.
medications.tramadol: An opioid painkiller for moderate to severe pain that also boosts serotonin and noradrenaline signalling.
medications.oxycodone: A strong opioid painkiller for severe pain, including cancer pain and pain after major surgery.
medications.chlorphenamine: A first-generation antihistamine, sold over the counter, that relieves hay fever.
medications.beclometasone: An inhaled corticosteroid taken every day to calm the airway inflammation of asthma and prevent attacks.
medications.influenza-vaccine: The yearly flu vaccine: an inactivated or live attenuated vaccine reformulated each season to match circulating influenza strains.
medications.iodinated-contrast: The iodine-containing dyes injected for CT scans and angiography that make blood vessels, organs and tumours show up.
medications.fluorodeoxyglucose-f18: The radioactive sugar used in most PET scans: cells that use a lot of glucose, such as many cancers, take it up and light up on the image.
medications.estradiol: The main natural oestrogen, given as tablets, patches, gel, spray or vaginal preparations to replace what the ovaries no longer make after the…
medications.testosterone: The main androgen, given as a gel, patch, injection or implant to replace what the testes cannot make in confirmed hypogonadism and as the…
medications.naproxen: Naproxen is a painkiller that also treats inflammation, used for conditions such as period pain, back pain, gout and arthritis.
medications.diclofenac: Diclofenac is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that eases pain and swelling in problems affecting joints, muscles and bones.
medications.lansoprazole: Lansoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that lowers stomach acid, used for indigestion, heartburn, reflux disease and stomach ulcers.
medications.esomeprazole: Esomeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that lowers the amount of acid the stomach makes.
medications.propranolol: Propranolol is a beta blocker used for heart problems such as high blood pressure, to help with some symptoms of anxiety and to prevent migraines.
medications.loratadine: A non-drowsy antihistamine that blocks the effects of histamine to relieve allergy symptoms.
medications.fexofenadine: Fexofenadine is a non-drowsy antihistamine that relieves allergy symptoms such as those of hay fever and hives by blocking the effects of histamine.
medications.codeine: Codeine is an opioid painkiller used for pain such as pain after an operation or injury.
medications.simvastatin: Simvastatin is a statin, a medicine that lowers cholesterol by reducing how much the liver makes.
medications.sumatriptan: Sumatriptan is a medicine used to treat migraines and cluster headaches once an attack has begun, and it does not stop migraines from starting.
medications.ondansetron: Ondansetron is an anti-sickness medicine used to prevent nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy, radiotherapy and surgery.
medications.metoclopramide: Metoclopramide is an anti-sickness medicine used to stop nausea (feeling sick) and vomiting (being sick).
medications.loperamide: Loperamide is a medicine for diarrhoea that slows the activity of the bowel so that stools firm up.
medications.lactulose: Lactulose is a laxative used to treat constipation, and it is also used for hepatic encephalopathy, a condition caused by severe liver disease.
medications.diazepam: Diazepam is a benzodiazepine, a type of medicine used to treat anxiety, muscle spasms and seizures.
medications.zopiclone: Zopiclone is a medicine used to treat insomnia, usually prescribed for just 2 to 4 weeks.
medications.doxycycline: Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic, available on prescription.
medications.flucloxacillin: A penicillin-type antibiotic, available on prescription, used for infections of the skin and wounds, bone infections and ear infections.
medications.co-amoxiclav: A penicillin antibiotic that combines amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, used for bacterial infections such as those of the ears, lungs, sinuses.
medications.metronidazole: An antibiotic used for bacterial infections of the skin, mouth and gums, and the vagina and pelvis, and the usual treatment for trichomoniasis.
medications.nitrofurantoin: Nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic that the NHS describes as a medicine for lower urinary tract infections such as cystitis.
medications.trimethoprim: Trimethoprim is an antibiotic used to treat and prevent urinary tract infections such as cystitis, and occasionally other infections.
medications.tamsulosin: Tamsulosin is an alpha blocker prescribed mainly for the urinary difficulties caused by an enlarged prostate gland.
medications.finasteride: Finasteride is a tablet that stops testosterone turning into the hormone DHT, used for an enlarged prostate and for male pattern hair loss.
medications.pregabalin: Pregabalin is a prescription medicine used for nerve pain, epilepsy and generalised anxiety disorder.
medications.gabapentin: A prescription medicine used to treat epilepsy and nerve pain.
medications.amitriptyline: Amitriptyline is a prescription-only medicine from a group called tricyclic antidepressants, used for nerve pain and to help prevent migraine.
medications.duloxetine: Duloxetine is an antidepressant medicine that is also used for anxiety and nerve pain.
medications.venlafaxine: Venlafaxine is an antidepressant called a serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), used for depression.
medications.mirtazapine: Mirtazapine is an antidepressant, prescribed mainly for depression and sometimes for obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) and anxiety.
medications.fluoxetine: Fluoxetine is an SSRI antidepressant, available only on prescription, that the NHS says is used for depression.
medications.dapagliflozin: Dapagliflozin is a prescription tablet from the SGLT2 inhibitor group, used for type 2 diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease.
medications.empagliflozin: Empagliflozin is a prescription medicine used to treat type 2 diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease.
medications.ezetimibe: Ezetimibe is a prescribed cholesterol-lowering medicine that works by reducing how much cholesterol the gut absorbs.
medications.gliclazide: Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea tablet prescribed for type 2 diabetes that prompts the pancreas to make more insulin.
medications.semaglutide: Semaglutide is a medicine used to manage type 2 diabetes (as Ozempic and Rybelsus) or to treat obesity (as Wegovy).
medications.spironolactone: Spironolactone is a diuretic, a medicine that helps reduce fluid build-up in the body.
medications.tirzepatide: Tirzepatide is a prescription medicine used to manage type 2 diabetes and to treat obesity.
medications.sildenafil: Sildenafil is a medicine used to treat erection problems and, sometimes, pulmonary hypertension.
medications.tadalafil: Tadalafil is a medicine mainly used to treat erection problems.
medications.combined-pill: The combined pill is a hormonal contraceptive that contains two hormones, oestrogen and a progestogen.
medications.aciclovir: Aciclovir is an antiviral medicine used for infections such as cold sores, shingles, chickenpox and genital herpes.
medications.fluconazole: Fluconazole is an antifungal medicine used for thrush and other fungal infections.
medications.hydroxychloroquine: Hydroxychloroquine is a medicine used to treat rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and some skin conditions.
medications.methotrexate: Methotrexate is an immunosuppressant used for inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis and Crohn's disease.
medications.montelukast: Montelukast is a prescription medicine that helps prevent asthma symptoms.

drug-classes.calcium-channel-blockers: Medicines that relax the muscle in artery walls (and, for some members.
drug-classes.ace-inhibitors: Medicines ending in -pril that block the enzyme which makes angiotensin II, lowering blood pressure.
drug-classes.angiotensin-receptor-blockers: Medicines ending in -sartan that block the receptor angiotensin II acts on.
drug-classes.beta-blockers: Medicines ending in -olol that shield the heart from adrenaline, slowing it and reducing its oxygen demand.
drug-classes.loop-diuretics: Powerful diuretics that make the kidneys excrete salt and water within an hour.
drug-classes.anticoagulants: Medicines that slow the clotting cascade to prevent and treat clots in veins and the heart: strokes in atrial fibrillation.
drug-classes.antiplatelets: Medicines that stop platelets clumping into the clots that block arteries.
drug-classes.nitrates: Vasodilators that relieve angina within minutes by relaxing veins and coronary arteries.
drug-classes.nsaids: Painkillers that also reduce inflammation and fever: ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac and the COX-2 selective coxibs.
drug-classes.non-opioid-analgesics: First-line painkillers without opioid or anti-inflammatory action: paracetamol (acetaminophen) above all.
drug-classes.opioids: Strong painkillers that act on the body's own endorphin receptors: morphine, codeine, tramadol, oxycodone, fentanyl.
drug-classes.biguanides: Metformin is the only biguanide in routine use and the first-line tablet for type 2 diabetes: it lowers glucose without causing hypoglycaemia or…
drug-classes.insulins: Injected replacements for the hormone the pancreas no longer makes or cannot make enough of: essential in type 1 diabetes and used in type 2…
drug-classes.thyroid-hormones: Synthetic thyroxine (levothyroxine) replaces what an underactive thyroid cannot make, restoring metabolic rate.
drug-classes.bronchodilators: Inhaled medicines that relax the muscle around the airways within minutes (salbutamol, terbutaline) or for about 12 hours (salmeterol.
drug-classes.corticosteroids: Synthetic versions of cortisol that switch off inflammation of any cause: inhaled for asthma, as tablets or injections for flares of many diseases.
drug-classes.proton-pump-inhibitors: The strongest acid-reducing medicines (omeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, esomeprazole).
drug-classes.penicillins: The oldest family of antibiotics and still the first choice for many chest, ear, throat, skin and dental infections: amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav.
drug-classes.antihistamines: Medicines that block histamine's H1 receptors to relieve hay fever, hives and itching.
drug-classes.ssris: The most widely used antidepressants (sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine), also first-line for anxiety disorders, panic.
drug-classes.xanthine-oxidase-inhibitors: Medicines that lower uric acid by blocking the enzyme that makes it, dissolving the crystals that cause gout attacks and tophi when taken every day.
drug-classes.bisphosphonates: Medicines that slow bone loss by disabling the cells that dissolve bone.
drug-classes.macrolides: Antibiotics that stop bacteria making proteins by binding the bacterial ribosome, used for chest, ear.
drug-classes.vaccines-influenza: Seasonal vaccines against influenza A and B, reformulated every year: inactivated injected vaccines for most people and a live attenuated nasal…
drug-classes.contrast-agents: Substances given to make blood vessels, organs, the gut or joints stand out on imaging: iodinated agents for X-ray and CT, gadolinium agents for MRI.
drug-classes.radiopharmaceuticals-diagnostic: Radioactive medicines given in tiny amounts so that a gamma camera or PET scanner can show where they accumulate: bone turnover.
drug-classes.androgens: Steroid hormones that act on the androgen receptor.
drug-classes.oestrogens: Steroid hormones that act on the oestrogen receptor.
drug-classes.triptans: Triptans are medicines for treating migraine attacks, and sumatriptan is the triptan covered on this site.
drug-classes.5-ht3-receptor-antagonists: Anti-sickness medicines that block 5-HT3 receptors; ondansetron is the member covered on this site.
drug-classes.dopamine-antagonist-antiemetics: Dopamine antagonist anti-sickness medicines are used to treat nausea and vomiting, and metoclopramide is the member covered on this site.
drug-classes.antimotility-agents: Antimotility agents are medicines that slow the bowel to treat diarrhoea, and loperamide is the member covered on this site.
drug-classes.osmotic-laxatives: Osmotic laxatives draw water into the bowel to soften poo; lactulose is the one covered on this site.
drug-classes.benzodiazepines: Benzodiazepines are depressant medicines that slow the central nervous system, and diazepam is the member covered on this site.
drug-classes.z-drugs: Z-drugs are sleeping medicines used for insomnia, and zopiclone is the member covered on this site.
drug-classes.tetracyclines: Tetracyclines are a group of antibiotics that stop bacteria from making the proteins they need to survive.
drug-classes.nitroimidazoles: Antibiotic and antiparasitic medicines, including metronidazole and tinidazole, that act on bacteria and parasites.
drug-classes.urinary-antibacterials: Antibiotics used for urinary tract infections.
drug-classes.alpha-blockers: Alpha blockers, also called alpha-adrenoreceptor antagonists, are medicines that relax muscle.
drug-classes.5-alpha-reductase-inhibitors: A group of medicines that stop testosterone turning into the hormone DHT; finasteride.
drug-classes.gabapentinoids: Gabapentinoids are the group that contains pregabalin and gabapentin, which are used for epilepsy and nerve pain.
drug-classes.tricyclic-antidepressants: Tricyclic antidepressants are a group of medicines that includes amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine and clomipramine.
drug-classes.snris: SNRIs are a group of antidepressants whose NHS examples are duloxetine and venlafaxine.
drug-classes.noradrenergic-and-specific-serotonergic-: The NHS groups antidepressants into types such as SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics and MAOIs.
drug-classes.cholesterol-absorption-inhibitors: Cholesterol absorption inhibitors are medicines that lower cholesterol by partly blocking its absorption in the small intestine.
drug-classes.glp-1-receptor-agonists: GLP-1 receptor agonists are medicines that imitate GLP-1, a hormone the body releases after eating.
drug-classes.mineralocorticoid-receptor-antagonists: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, also called aldosterone antagonists, are medicines that act against the hormone aldosterone.
drug-classes.sglt2-inhibitors: SGLT2 inhibitors are tablets used for type 2 diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease.
drug-classes.sulfonylureas: Sulfonylureas are tablets for type 2 diabetes that prompt the pancreas to make more insulin.
drug-classes.pde5-inhibitors: PDE5 inhibitors are medicines that include sildenafil and tadalafil, used mainly for erection problems.
drug-classes.combined-hormonal-contraceptives: Combined hormonal contraceptives contain both an oestrogen and a progestogen, and include the combined pill, a skin patch and a vaginal ring.
drug-classes.nucleoside-antivirals: Antiviral medicines used for herpes virus infections such as cold sores, shingles, chickenpox and genital herpes.
drug-classes.azole-antifungals: Antifungal medicines, including fluconazole, used for thrush and other fungal infections.
drug-classes.antimalarial-dmards: MedlinePlus places hydroxychloroquine in a group of medicines called antimalarials and also describes it as an antirheumatic drug.
drug-classes.antimetabolite-dmards: Antimetabolite DMARDs are a group of disease-modifying medicines; methotrexate is the member covered on this site.
drug-classes.leukotriene-receptor-antagonists: Montelukast is a prescription medicine that helps prevent asthma symptoms.

biomarkers.haemoglobin: The iron-containing protein inside red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to every tissue.
biomarkers.haematocrit: The fraction of blood volume made up of red cells, reported as a percentage or a ratio.
biomarkers.mcv: The average size of a red blood cell, calculated by the analyser during a full blood count.
biomarkers.white-cell-count: The total number of white blood cells in a volume of blood: the immune cells that fight infection and drive inflammation.
biomarkers.neutrophils: The most numerous white blood cell and the first responder to bacterial infection.
biomarkers.lymphocytes: The white blood cells that carry adaptive immunity (B cells that make antibodies, T cells that direct the response and kill infected cells).
biomarkers.platelets: Small cell fragments that plug damaged vessel walls and start the clotting cascade.
biomarkers.hba1c: Haemoglobin that has glucose attached to it.
biomarkers.glucose: The concentration of glucose, the body's main circulating fuel, in blood at the moment of sampling.
biomarkers.troponin: A protein of the contractile apparatus of heart muscle cells that leaks into blood when those cells are injured.
biomarkers.bnp: Hormones released by the heart's ventricles when their walls are stretched by high pressure or volume.
biomarkers.total-cholesterol: The sum of all the cholesterol carried in blood by lipoproteins: LDL, HDL and the remainder.
biomarkers.ldl-cholesterol: The cholesterol carried by low-density lipoprotein, the particle that deposits cholesterol in artery walls and drives atherosclerosis.
biomarkers.hdl-cholesterol: The cholesterol carried by high-density lipoprotein, the particle that collects cholesterol from tissues and artery walls and returns it to the liver.
biomarkers.triglycerides: The main form in which fat is stored and transported: three fatty acids on a glycerol backbone.
biomarkers.alt: An enzyme concentrated in liver cells that leaks into blood when they are injured.
biomarkers.ast: An enzyme found in liver cells but also in heart, skeletal muscle, kidney, brain and red cells.
biomarkers.alp: An enzyme made mainly by the cells lining the bile ducts and by bone-forming cells.
biomarkers.ggt: A membrane enzyme of bile-duct and liver cells that rises with cholestasis, alcohol and many medicines.
biomarkers.bilirubin: The yellow pigment made when old red cells are broken down, processed by the liver and excreted in bile.
biomarkers.albumin: The most abundant protein in blood, made by the liver.
biomarkers.creatinine: A waste product of muscle metabolism produced at a steady rate and cleared almost entirely by the kidneys.
biomarkers.egfr: An estimate of how many millilitres of blood the kidneys filter each minute, calculated from creatinine together with age and sex.
biomarkers.urea: The nitrogen-containing waste the liver makes from protein breakdown, cleared by the kidneys.
biomarkers.potassium: The main positively charged ion inside cells; only about 2% is in the blood, but that small fraction sets the electrical excitability of nerves.
biomarkers.sodium: The main positively charged ion of the fluid outside cells and the chief determinant of blood osmolality.
biomarkers.tsh: The pituitary hormone that drives the thyroid gland.
biomarkers.free-t4: The unbound fraction of thyroxine, the main hormone the thyroid gland secretes.
biomarkers.crp: A protein the liver pours into blood within hours of any significant inflammation, infection or tissue injury.
biomarkers.ferritin: The protein that stores iron inside cells; the small amount in blood mirrors the body's iron reserve.
biomarkers.inr: The prothrombin time expressed as a standardised ratio, the number used to dose warfarin and to gauge the liver's production of clotting factors.
biomarkers.vitamin-b12: The vitamin, absorbed with intrinsic factor in the last part of the small intestine.
biomarkers.folate: The B vitamin from green vegetables and fortified foods that cells need to make DNA; deficiency causes anaemia with large red cells and.
biomarkers.vitamin-d-25-oh: The storage form of vitamin D that the liver makes, the best single measure of vitamin D status and the value the vitamin D test reports.
biomarkers.hcg: The hormone made from implantation onwards by the trophoblast, the tissue that becomes the placenta.
biomarkers.oestradiol: The main oestrogen of the reproductive years, made chiefly by the growing ovarian follicle and, in smaller amounts.
biomarkers.testosterone: The principal androgen, made mainly by the testes and in smaller amounts by the ovaries and adrenal glands.

targets.l-type-calcium-channel: A voltage-gated channel in the membrane of smooth-muscle and heart-muscle cells that lets calcium in when the cell is electrically excited.
targets.at1-receptor: The receptor through which angiotensin II constricts arteries, releases aldosterone and drives the thickening of heart and vessel walls.
targets.angiotensin-converting-enzyme: The enzyme on the surface of blood-vessel lining cells, above all in the lungs.
targets.hmg-coa-reductase: The enzyme that controls the speed of cholesterol synthesis in the liver.
targets.cox-1: The 'housekeeping' form of cyclo-oxygenase, present all the time in platelets, the stomach lining and the kidney.
targets.cox-2: The inducible form of cyclo-oxygenase, switched on at sites of injury and inflammation and in the brain during fever.
targets.serotonin-transporter: The pump on the presynaptic nerve ending that clears serotonin from the synapse after it has been released.
targets.beta-1-adrenoceptor: The receptor in heart muscle and the heart's pacemaker tissue through which adrenaline and noradrenaline speed the heart and strengthen its…
targets.beta-2-adrenoceptor: The receptor on airway smooth muscle through which adrenaline relaxes the bronchi.
targets.proton-pump: The enzyme in the stomach's parietal cells that pumps acid into the stomach as the final step of acid secretion.
targets.penicillin-binding-proteins: Bacterial enzymes that cross-link the peptidoglycan mesh of the cell wall as bacteria grow.
targets.bacterial-ribosome: The protein-making machinery of bacteria, built differently enough from the human ribosome to be a selective drug target.
targets.hepatic-glucose-production: The liver's manufacture and release of glucose between meals, from lactate, amino acids and glycerol.
targets.mu-opioid-receptor: The receptor through which morphine and the other opioids relieve pain, and also the one responsible for their sedation, slowed breathing.
targets.h1-receptor: The receptor through which histamine, released from mast cells in an allergic reaction, causes itching, sneezing, a runny nose, swelling and hives.
targets.vitamin-k-epoxide-reductase: The liver enzyme that recycles vitamin K so it can activate clotting factors II, VII, IX and X.
targets.factor-xa: The clotting enzyme at the junction of the two arms of the coagulation cascade, which converts prothrombin into thrombin.
targets.nkcc2: The transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle that reabsorbs sodium, potassium and chloride from the filtrate.
targets.xanthine-oxidase: The enzyme that makes uric acid from the purines released when cells and DNA break down.
targets.glucocorticoid-receptor: The receptor inside almost every cell through which cortisol, and corticosteroid medicines such as prednisolone and inhaled beclometasone.
targets.thyroid-hormone-receptor: The nuclear receptor in nearly every cell through which triiodothyronine (T3) sets the pace of metabolism, heart rate, temperature and growth.
targets.insulin-receptor: The receptor on muscle, fat and liver cells through which insulin moves glucose out of the blood and into storage.
targets.androgen-receptor: The nuclear receptor through which testosterone and dihydrotestosterone act on the genitals, prostate, muscle, bone, bone marrow, skin.
targets.oestrogen-receptor: The nuclear receptor through which oestradiol acts on the uterus, breast, bone, blood vessels, liver and brain.

first-aid.cpr: When the heart stops, blood stops reaching the brain and brain cells begin to die within minutes.
first-aid.heart-attack: A coronary artery has blocked and heart muscle is dying.
first-aid.stroke: A blood vessel in the brain has blocked or burst.
first-aid.choking: Food or an object has lodged in the larynx or trachea.
first-aid.severe-bleeding: An adult has about 5 litres of blood and can lose a fifth before the body's compensation fails; a severed artery can do that in minutes.
first-aid.burns: Heat keeps damaging skin for minutes after the source is removed, so cooling with running water is the treatment that changes outcomes.
first-aid.fractures: A broken bone is rarely life-threatening in itself, but the sharp ends can cut vessels and nerves.
first-aid.sprains: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament (the bands that hold a joint together); a strain is a stretched or torn muscle or tendon.
first-aid.fainting: A faint is a brief loss of consciousness because blood pressure drops and the brain is starved of blood for a few seconds.
first-aid.seizures: A seizure is a burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain.
first-aid.heatstroke: Heat exhaustion is the body struggling to shed heat: sweaty, weak and dizzy, but still thinking clearly.
first-aid.hypothermia: Hypothermia is a core temperature below 35°C.
first-aid.poisoning: A poison is anything taken in a quantity that harms: medicines (paracetamol, opioids, antidepressants), household chemicals, plants, carbon monoxide.
first-aid.allergic-reactions: Anaphylaxis is a whole-body allergic reaction, usually within minutes of a food, sting or drug.
first-aid.electric-shock: Electricity passing through the body can stop the heart, paralyse breathing muscles.
first-aid.wound-care: Most cuts and grazes heal on their own if they are cleaned, closed and kept covered.

health.exercise: Movement is the single intervention that improves almost every organ system at once: it strengthens the heart, lowers blood pressure and blood sugar.
health.sleep: Sleep is not downtime: the brain clears metabolic waste, consolidates memory and resets emotional circuits, while the body repairs tissue.
health.nutrition: Food supplies energy, the building blocks for every tissue, and the vitamins and minerals that enzymes need.
health.weight: Body fat is an active endocrine organ.
health.smoking: Tobacco smoke delivers nicotine, an addictive stimulant, in a cloud of 7,000 chemicals including 70 known carcinogens, carbon monoxide and tar.
health.alcohol: Alcohol is absorbed from the stomach and small intestine, distributed through body water and processed by the liver at roughly one unit an hour.
health.hydration: Water makes up about 60% of an adult's body and is the medium for every chemical reaction, the carrier for every nutrient and waste product.
health.transgender-health: Trans and non-binary people need the same care as everyone else plus a few things specific to their bodies and treatment: monitoring of…
health.womens-health: Women's health covers the care of organs that change every month and at every stage of life: periods, contraception and fertility, pregnancy.

blog.ace-inhibitors-arbs-and-amlodipine-compa: ARBs work much like ACE inhibitors but do not typically cause a dry cough; amlodipine relaxes artery walls and can cause ankle swelling.
blog.alcohol-and-antibiotics: It depends on the antibiotic: the NHS says moderate drinking is unlikely to cause problems with common ones, but firm warnings exist for a few.
blog.alcohol-units-and-low-risk-drinking: The UK Chief Medical Officers advise adults not to regularly drink more than 14 units a week, spread over three days or more.
blog.altitude-sickness-symptoms-and-preventio: Altitude sickness is illness from being high up with less oxygen; the NHS says mild cases ease with rest, and going up slowly helps prevent it.
blog.anaphylaxis-and-adrenaline-auto-injector: Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction; the NHS describes adrenaline, calling 999 and hospital care.
blog.antenatal-care-on-the-nhs: The NHS offers antenatal appointments with a midwife, two ultrasound scans and optional screening tests.
blog.anxiety-signs-and-treatment: Anxiety becomes a health problem when worry is hard to control and affects daily life.
blog.asthma-and-copd-how-they-differ: Asthma is a long-term airway condition whose symptoms come and go; COPD is mostly smoking-related and tends to get worse over time.
blog.asthma-in-children-signs-and-nhs-advice: Asthma in children brings wheeze, cough and a tight chest; the NHS says to call 999 if the reliever is not helping during an attack.
blog.back-pain-what-helps-and-when-to-get-hel: Most back pain settles with time and staying active helps, but new numbness around the genitals or changes in bladder or bowel control need urgent…
blog.being-active-with-a-long-term-health-con: UK guidance describes building up activity gradually from the current level.
blog.bladder-control-problems-types-and-help: The NHS lists stress, urge, overflow and total incontinence; a GP can assess it, and treatment usually starts with non-drug options.
blog.bleeding-after-menopause-and-between-per: Any vaginal bleeding after the menopause should be checked by a GP.
blog.blood-clots-on-long-flights-dvt-risk: Long journeys can raise the chance of a leg blood clot (DVT); the NHS and TravelHealthPro describe moving, drinking water and sometimes stockings.
blog.blood-in-urine-causes-and-what-happens-n: Blood in the urine is not usually serious, but the NHS advises seeing a GP every time, even if the amount is small.
blog.blood-pressure-at-home-how-it-works: The NHS says blood pressure can be checked at home with a monitor, with the cuff on the upper arm and the person sitting with their back supported.
blog.blood-test-preparation-and-fasting: Some blood tests need fasting or a change to what you eat, drink or take beforehand; the person who arranges the test should say which applies.
blog.blood-transfusion-why-and-how-it-is-done: A blood transfusion gives red blood cells, plasma or platelets from a donor to someone who has lost blood or has a condition affecting their blood.
blog.bone-health-keeping-bones-strong: NHS pages link bone health to weight-bearing exercise, calcium, vitamin D, not smoking and keeping alcohol low.
blog.bone-marrow-biopsy-what-happens-and-why: A bone marrow biopsy takes a small sample of marrow, usually from the back of the hip bone.
blog.breast-lump-what-happens-after-you-find-: Most breast lumps are harmless, but the NHS advises seeing a GP about any new lump so it can be checked.
blog.breast-screening-mammogram-what-to-expec: NHS breast screening uses mammograms to look for breast cancer in people without symptoms.
blog.burns-and-scalds-first-aid-and-when-to-g: Cooling a burn under running water for 20 minutes is the first step; the NHS says large, deep, facial, chemical or electrical burns need A&E or 999.
blog.cardiovascular-service-framework-england: The government and NHS England have published a cardiovascular disease framework that aims to cut premature deaths from heart disease and stroke by…
blog.caring-for-someone-with-dementia-nhs-adv: The NHS suggests a daily routine, and says carers can ask the council for a free carer's assessment.
blog.cdc-2026-2027-respiratory-season-outlook: The US CDC's outlook dated 23 September 2026 expects the peak of combined COVID-19, flu and RSV hospital admissions to be similar to last season.
blog.cervical-screening-what-to-expect: Cervical screening checks a sample from the cervix for high-risk HPV.
blog.chest-pain-causes-and-when-to-get-help: Most chest pain does not come from the heart, but sudden pain that does not ease or spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back needs a 999 call.
blog.childhood-rashes-chickenpox-measles-hand: Chickenpox, measles and hand, foot and mouth all cause rashes in children, but their other signs and the advice on getting help differ.
blog.choking-what-the-nhs-and-resus-council-d: First-aid guidance describes back blows and abdominal thrusts for severe choking, 999 if the blockage stays.
blog.cholesterol-and-diet-what-the-nhs-says: The NHS says cutting down on saturated fat can help lower cholesterol.
blog.cholesterol-blood-test-results-explained: A cholesterol test reports total, HDL and non-HDL cholesterol plus triglycerides, and doctors read them with other risk factors.
blog.choose-the-right-nhs-service-999-111-gp-: The NHS says 999 is for life-threatening emergencies and NHS 111 for urgent problems or when unsure, with pharmacies.
blog.colic-in-babies-what-it-is-and-what-help: Colic is a baby crying a lot with no obvious cause; NHS guidance says it usually gets better by around 3 or 4 months.
blog.colonoscopy-preparation-and-what-happens: A colonoscopy uses a thin camera to look inside the large bowel.
blog.contraception-methods-the-nhs-lists-comp: The NHS lists hormonal, coil, barrier, emergency and permanent methods; they differ in how they work and how long they last.
blog.coronary-angiogram-what-happens-and-risk: A coronary angiogram is an X-ray test that uses dye to show narrowed or blocked heart arteries.
blog.ct-scan-what-to-expect: A CT scan uses X-rays and a computer to build slice pictures of the body.
blog.cystoscopy-what-happens-and-what-to-expe: A cystoscopy uses a thin camera passed through the urethra to look inside the bladder.
blog.dementia-early-signs-and-assessment: Early signs of dementia include memory loss, trouble with familiar tasks and confusion about time or place.
blog.depression-signs-and-getting-help: Depression is more than feeling unhappy for a few days.
blog.dhsc-under-18-sales-ban-vapes-nicotine-p: New rules took effect on 29 October 2026 making it illegal to sell any vape or non-medicinal nicotine product to anyone under 18.
blog.diabetes-foot-care-daily-checks-and-annu: Diabetes can reduce feeling in the feet and slow healing, so UK sources describe daily checks and an annual foot check.
blog.dizziness-and-vertigo-causes-and-warning: Dizziness is common and has many causes, from inner ear problems to low blood pressure.
blog.dxa-bone-density-scan-explained: A DXA scan measures bone density, usually at the hip and spine, using low-dose X-rays.
blog.early-pregnancy-symptoms-and-contacting-: The NHS says a missed period is the earliest sign of pregnancy, and many areas let people refer themselves to a midwife.
blog.eating-well-with-type-2-diabetes: Diabetes UK says there is no special diet only for type 2 diabetes, and NICE advises the same healthy balanced eating as for everyone.
blog.eatwell-guide-healthy-eating: The Eatwell Guide shows the proportions of food groups in a balanced UK diet, with fruit.
blog.ecg-what-it-records-and-shows: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity through patches on the skin.
blog.echocardiogram-types-and-what-it-shows: An echocardiogram uses ultrasound to picture the heart.
blog.egfr-and-creatinine-kidney-blood-tests: Creatinine and eGFR show how well the kidneys filter blood, and kidney disease is confirmed only when abnormal results persist.
blog.erectile-dysfunction-causes-and-when-to-: Erection problems are common and can have physical causes, and the NHS advises seeing a GP if they keep happening.
blog.eye-tests-who-gets-a-free-nhs-sight-test: The NHS says everyone should have regular eye tests, at least every 2 years, and lists who can have a free NHS sight test in England.
blog.falls-in-older-people-reducing-risk: Strength and balance exercises and simple changes at home can lower the risk of falls in older people, according to the NHS.

blog.fda-generic-climara-pro-hormone-patch: The US FDA approved the first generic version of the Climara Pro once-weekly patch, which combines estradiol and levonorgestrel, on 20 October 2026.
blog.fda-hibsago-chronic-hepatitis-b: The US FDA approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) on 20 October 2026, the first antisense oligonucleotide approved for chronic hepatitis B in certain adults.
blog.fda-imlunestrant-abemaciclib-breast-canc: The US FDA approved imlunestrant (Inluriyo) with abemaciclib on 18 September 2026 for ER-positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated advanced breast cancer.
blog.fda-injectafer-boxed-warning-low-phospha: The US FDA said on 1 September 2026 that it added a boxed warning to Injectafer (ferric carboxymaltose) about the risk of low blood phosphate.
blog.fda-stelara-pediatric-ulcerative-colitis: The US FDA approved Stelara (ustekinumab) for children aged 2 and older with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, in August 2026.
blog.fda-thyroid-tablets-lot-recall-vitruvias: Vitruvias Therapeutics announced a US recall of one lot of Thyroid Tablets, USP 30 mg on 21 August 2026 because of possible superpotency.
blog.fda-trutakna-iga-nephropathy: The US FDA granted accelerated approval to Trutakna (atacicept-vymj) on 7 July 2026 to reduce protein in the urine in adults with primary IgA…
blog.fda-tucatinib-her2-breast-cancer-mainten: The US FDA approved tucatinib (Tukysa) on 7 October 2026 with trastuzumab and pertuzumab as maintenance treatment for advanced HER2-positive breast…
blog.fda-zidesamtinib-ros1-lung-cancer: The US FDA approved zidesamtinib (Jideytro) on 22 July 2026 for adults with previously treated ROS1-positive non-small cell lung cancer.
blog.feeling-sick-and-vomiting-in-adults: NHS inform says vomiting in adults usually lasts only 1 or 2 days, but blood in vomit means calling 999 or going to A&E.
blog.fever-in-adults-causes-and-when-to-get-h: A high temperature in adults is usually a sign of infection and often settles at home.
blog.fever-in-children-when-to-get-help: Most fevers in children can be looked after at home.
blog.flu-jab-booking-opens-winter-2026: NHS England says national booking for this winter's flu jab is open.
blog.flu-or-cold-how-they-differ: Flu tends to start faster and feel worse than a cold, with fever, aches and exhaustion; a cold mostly stays in the nose and throat.
blog.flu-vaccinations-ten-million-october-202: The Department of Health and Social Care says more than 10 million flu vaccinations have been delivered in England.
blog.gastroscopy-what-happens-and-what-to-exp: A gastroscopy uses a thin camera to look at the gullet and stomach.
blog.general-anaesthetic-before-during-and-af: A general anaesthetic puts a person into controlled unconsciousness for surgery.
blog.grief-and-bereavement-what-to-expect: Grief is a natural response to loss, and the NHS says feelings usually ease gradually.
blog.hba1c-test-what-it-shows: The HbA1c test shows average blood glucose over the past two to three months and is used to diagnose and monitor diabetes.
blog.head-injury-and-concussion-when-to-get-h: Most head injuries are not serious, but the NHS says being knocked out and not waking, a fit or being unable to stay awake need a 999 call.
blog.head-lice-and-nits-what-the-nhs-says: Head lice are tiny insects in the hair.
blog.headache-types-causes-and-warning-signs: Tension-type headache is the most common type, and a headache that starts suddenly and is very severe needs a 999 call.
blog.healthy-weight-bmi-explained: BMI is an NHS check on whether weight suits height, but it cannot tell muscle from fat, so waist size and a GP discussion add to it.
blog.hearing-loss-causes-tests-and-help: Gradual hearing loss is common and a GP can arrange hearing tests.
